extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; scholars of English allegory and Bunyan/Victorian literature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative points for judging allegorical/narrative works (here exemplified by Bunyan's The Holy War), focusing on vividness, consistency, theological handling, symbolism, characterization, and dramatic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness and internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The story runs on firmly and clearly. It is vivid, consistent in itself, and held well within the limits of human nature and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works of fiction (especially allegory) succeed when they are lively and internally coherent and when their action remains believable within human experience; failure to maintain this weakens the art. Example: the earlier parts of Bunyan's tale are praised for these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of facts (impact without allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question to us is if the facts are true. If true they require no allegories to touch either our hearts or our intellects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a narrative's underlying facts or moral truths are convincing, the work needs less ornamental allegory to move readers. Implication: excessive allegorizing may be unnecessary or even distracting when the facts themselves are powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness in portraying the Divine (avoid theatricalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of making the Almighty into a stage actor: Bunyan (like Milton) is censured for representing the Father and Son in a manner resembling theatrical representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacred subjects should be handled with reverence; dramatizing divine councils or making God appear as a theatrical figure undermines seriousness. The critic suggests leaving 'plans of salvation' to pulpit or restrained treatment rather than stage-like presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory's permissible scope (do not cross-question too minutely)
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegory must not be cross-questioned too minutely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the intentional simplifications and symbolic choices of allegory; probing every literal implication can be a category error. Critics should evaluate within the allegory's intended symbolic range rather than demand literal realism at every turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apt naming and personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of illustrative, characterizing names (e.g., Mr. Incredulity, Mr. Haughty, Mr. Falsepeace) is an effective device; Bunyan 'was never at a loss' for such names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-chosen, emblematic names and personifications can efficiently convey moral qualities and social arrangements; arrangement (e.g., eldest/youngest) can also reinforce meaning. This is praised as a strength of Bunyan's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic completeness and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should contain the parts of a complete drama—the fair beginning, the perils, the struggles, and the final victory of good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfying allegorical drama presents a clear arc: establishment, conflict, climax, and resolution. The critic notes Bunyan achieves this overall dramatic shape, which is an important standard of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of emblems and symbolic imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Emblems (e.g., banners bearing the Book of the Law, a burning furnace, a fruitless tree with an axe) should clearly represent theological or thematic points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic images and emblems are appropriate and effective when they concretely convey doctrinal themes (such as the terrors of Sinai or the covenant of works). The critic cites these emblems as meaningful, not mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in explanation (avoid over-ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bunyan was 'too ambitious to explain the inexplicable'—ambitious exposition can push an allegory into perilous ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid over-explaining mysteries or theological complexities in allegory; excessive ambition to account for the inexplicable can harm the work's art. Leave some elements suggestive rather than exhaustively rationalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of drama and reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain reverence while dramatizing sacred history—e.g., Bunyan 'was too reverent to imitate the Mystery Plays' and thus avoids certain theatrical depictions of sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find a middle path between vivid dramatic representation and appropriate reverence for religious subjects; some events (like central sacrifice) may be better treated as assumed background than stage action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate delegation of doctrinal exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary figures (e.g., the Recorder/Conscience) must 'confine' themselves to moral and civil teaching and not presume to reveal 'high and supernatural mysteries' which belong only to the higher divine source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In allegory and didactic fiction, distinguish between moral instruction (legitimate for many characters) and revelation of supernatural doctrine (reserved, in the allegory, for the highest authority). This preserves theological order and plausibility within the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of justice and moral consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals of judgment and punishment should reflect moral purpose and the limits of temporal justice (e.g., Diabolonians executed but unbelief can escape and return).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice scenes should be dramatically effective yet nuanced: exemplary punishment may be depicted while acknowledging moral complexities (such as the persistence or return of certain vices). The critic applauds Bunyan's courtroom and execution scenes as vivid but notes their provisional character.
